assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's strontium clock work, moved timekeeping to the 10^-18 level. This is the clearest case of an advance in what can be measured and how accurately: it opens relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and a redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and demonstrated the early clock; Ye's group drove the record accuracy and stability. The credited pair is a natural two-person prize. Others (e.g. Hall and Hänsch frequency combs, Ludlow, Lemonde) were already recognised or are not on the list, so the pair is clean.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed by many groups worldwide at the 10^-18 level; the physics is stable and the technology is in international comparisons. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views clocks as a distinct enough step beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes in precision spectroscopy.
Credit for the original magic-wavelength idea versus the later accuracy milestones is stated from memory and not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapped-ion quantum computation began with the Cirac-Zoller gate proposal and was realised experimentally with high-fidelity gates, entanglement and digital and analogue simulation. It is a foundational platform for quantum information with deep roots in laser spectroscopy and coherent control.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the decisive theoretical proposal; Blatt led the experimental realisation and scale-up. Other leaders (Monroe, Wineland, already honoured in 2012) leave some allocation tension, but the supplied trio is coherent.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of independent confirmation across several groups and a mature commercial trajectory. Timely.
uncertainties: Overlap with Wineland's 2012 recognition and with Monroe's contribution is unresolved.
The Cirac-Zoller gate itself is no longer the leading experimental gate, so credit may be better framed around the proposal plus experiments.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Hubbard model and its relatives with tunable parameters, including the superfluid to Mott transition and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy, giving access to many-body physics that is intractable classically.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch, Cirac) provided the theory; Greiner and Bloch gave the Mott-insulator observation and microscopy; Esslinger and others made important contributions with fermions. The list has five names and only three can be selected, so Esslinger and Cirac are left out, a real attribution tension.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed across many laboratories; the field is mature and now has quantum-simulation output of wide use.
uncertainties: Selecting three of five credited names omits Esslinger and Cirac, which could be seen as unfair.
Overlap with the Rydberg and trapped-ion quantum-simulation candidates may complicate the allocation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond turned a solid-state defect into a room-temperature quantum bit and sensor of magnetic fields, temperature and strain at the nanoscale, with applications in biology and materials. It sits squarely in the measurement-limits theme.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko demonstrated optical detection of single NV spins and coherent control; Lukin contributed decisive proposals and demonstrations of NV-based sensing and quantum registers. A fair three-person configuration, though Awschalom, Hanson and others also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced and now commercial; interpretation is stable. Timely.
uncertainties: Several other groups (Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby, Walsworth) have strong claims, so the credit boundary is arguable.
Overlap with B001, which covers solid-state spin-photon interfaces.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry gives inertial and gravitational sensing and tests of fundamental physics at extreme accuracy, applying matter-wave coherence to measurement of gravity, rotation and constants.
assessment.attribution: Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich (with Chu) are early central figures; Chu already shared the 1997 prize for laser cooling, which complicates the story. Schmiedmayer is also credited but left out.
assessment.maturity: Well established, with commercial gravimeters and precision tests, though the strongest fundamental-physics payoff, such as a decisive test beyond general relativity, is still pending.
uncertainties: Steven Chu's previous prize and his role in atom interferometry are not within the credited names.
Whether the field has delivered a landmark discovery versus technique is open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution founded quantum cryptography: BB84 and E91 turned quantum nonlocality and no-cloning into a practical information-theoretic security concept. Clear and original, and a link to the 2022 Bell-inequality prize.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard created BB84; Ekert independently proposed entanglement-based QKD. The credited list contains duplicate spellings of Ekert, which I treat as one person; I use the spelling 'Artur Ekert'.
assessment.maturity: Conceptual maturity is high and commercial and satellite experiments exist; however, practical deployment is still limited and the prize-relevant impact is mostly conceptual.
uncertainties: The duplicated Ekert spelling signals possible attribution noise in the supplied credit.
Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is not credited and may matter.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The titanium-sapphire gain medium and passive mode-locking made femtosecond lasers practical and underlie much of ultrafast science and frequency-comb work. Impact is vast, though the question is whether this is a physics discovery or an enabling invention.
assessment.attribution: Moulton developed Ti:sapphire; Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode-locking; Keller developed SESAMs. Three distinct contributions fit a three-person split, though the Kerr-lens work also involved Spence and Keller.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature; ubiquitous across laboratories, and in part already honoured through the chirped-pulse amplification and attosecond prizes.
uncertainties: Overlap with 2018 and 2023 recognition of ultrafast optics may reduce novelty.
Allocation among Kerr-lens inventors (Sibbett, Spence, Keller) is contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable Rydberg-atom arrays use optical tweezers and blockade interactions to build large controllable quantum simulators and emerging processors, with demonstrations of exotic phases and logical-qubit operations.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across five names; I select Browaeys, Lukin and Saffman for experimental and proposal contributions, leaving Zoller (already listed under other candidates) and Grangier. This is a hard split.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly maturing but young; independent confirmation by several groups exists, while long-term stability of the interpretation and impact is less settled than for the older candidates. Possibly premature.
uncertainties: Premature relative to other AMO candidates.
Five-way credit cannot be reduced to three without leaving out major contributors.
